claim: Systems consolidation theories propose coordinated reactivation between hippocampus and cortex as a mechanism that enables behavioral integration of related memories.
source: Systems consolidation theories propose two mechanisms that enable the behavioral integration of related memories: coordinated reactivation between hippocampus and cortex, and the emergence of cortical traces that reflect overlap across memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established theoretical frameworks in systems consolidation.

claim: Systems consolidation theories propose the emergence of cortical traces that reflect overlap across memories as a mechanism that enables behavioral integration of related memories.
source: Systems consolidation theories propose two mechanisms that enable the behavioral integration of related memories: coordinated reactivation between hippocampus and cortex, and the emergence of cortical traces that reflect overlap across memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established theoretical frameworks in systems consolidation.

claim: There is limited empirical evidence linking coordinated reactivation and cortical trace emergence to behavioral integration over time.
source: However, there is limited empirical evidence that links these mechanisms to the emergence of behavioral integration over time.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature based on the authors' review.

claim: Response times during a recognition task reflected behavioral priming between objects that never occurred together in time but belonged to overlapping sequences.
source: Assessment of behavioral integration showed that response times during a recognition task reflected behavioral priming between objects that never occurred together in time but belonged to overlapping sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the recognition priming task described in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral priming between objects from overlapping sequences was consolidation-dependent and only emerged for sequences learned 24 hr prior to the test.
source: This priming was consolidation-dependent and only emerged for sequences learned 24 hr prior to the test.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing recent and remote learning conditions.

claim: Behavioral integration was related to changes in neural pattern similarity in the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Critically, behavioral integration was related to changes in neural pattern similarity in the medial prefrontal cortex and increases in post-learning rest connectivity between the posterior hippocampus and lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses between behavioral priming and mPFC pattern similarity changes.

claim: Behavioral integration was related to increases in post-learning rest connectivity between the posterior hippocampus and lateral occipital cortex.
source: Critically, behavioral integration was related to changes in neural pattern similarity in the medial prefrontal cortex and increases in post-learning rest connectivity between the posterior hippocampus and lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses between behavioral priming and hippocampal-LOC connectivity.

claim: Memories with a shared predictive structure become behaviorally integrated through a consolidation-related restructuring of the learned sequences.
source: These findings suggest that memories with a shared predictive structure become behaviorally integrated through a consolidation-related restructuring of the learned sequences, providing insight into the relationship between different consolidation mechanisms that support behavioral integration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: After periods involving consolidation, episodic memories undergo transformations that allow individuals to integrate across overlapping experiences.
source: There are now abundant demonstrations that after periods involving consolidation, episodic memories undergo transformations that allow individuals to integrate across overlapping experiences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on consolidation-dependent integration.

claim: Enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation includes transitive inference.
source: Examples of enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation include transitive inference (Ellenbogen et al., 2007; Lau et al., 2010; Werchan and Gómez, 2013), the extraction of statistical regularities (Wagner et al., 2004; Durrant et al., 2011; Durrant et al., 2011; Sweegers et al., 2014; Batterink and Paller, 2017), category learning (Djonlagic et al., 2009; Graveline and Wamsley, 2017), and more (for reviews, see Chatburn et al., 2014; Lerner and Gluck, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies demonstrating transitive inference after consolidation.

claim: Enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation includes the extraction of statistical regularities.
source: Examples of enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation include transitive inference (Ellenbogen et al., 2007; Lau et al., 2010; Werchan and Gómez, 2013), the extraction of statistical regularities (Wagner et al., 2004; Durrant et al., 2011; Durrant et al., 2011; Sweegers et al., 2014; Batterink and Paller, 2017), category learning (Djonlagic et al., 2009; Graveline and Wamsley, 2017), and more (for reviews, see Chatburn et al., 2014; Lerner and Gluck, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies demonstrating statistical learning after consolidation.

claim: Enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation includes category learning.
source: Examples of enhanced behavioral integration with consolidation include transitive inference (Ellenbogen et al., 2007; Lau et al., 2010; Werchan and Gómez, 2013), the extraction of statistical regularities (Wagner et al., 2004; Durrant et al., 2011; Durrant et al., 2011; Sweegers et al., 2014; Batterink and Paller, 2017), category learning (Djonlagic et al., 2009; Graveline and Wamsley, 2017), and more (for reviews, see Chatburn et al., 2014; Lerner and Gluck, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies demonstrating category learning after consolidation.

claim: Memories initially supported by the hippocampus become distributed across the cortex through ongoing, coordinated reactivation of prior experiences.
source: Theories of systems-level consolidation posit that memories initially supported by the hippocampus become distributed across the cortex, through ongoing, coordinated reactivation of prior experiences (Nadel et al., 2000; Squire et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational theories of systems consolidation.

claim: Memory traces ultimately learned by cortex are highly structured and integrated representations built up from many overlapping experiences.
source: Through this reactivation, the memory traces that are ultimately learned by cortex are thought to be highly structured and integrated representations built up from many overlapping experiences (McClelland et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work on cortical memory representations.

claim: Trace Transformation Theory posits that neural integration is accompanied by a psychological transformation such that memories supported by cortex are more gist-like and reflect shared aspects across multiple events.
source: One class of theories posits that neural integration is accompanied by a psychological transformation such that memories supported by cortex are more gist-like and reflect the shared aspects across multiple events (Trace Transformation Theory (TTT); Sekeres et al., 2018a; Winocur et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Trace Transformation Theory.

claim: Damage to medial prefrontal cortex impairs associative inference in humans.
source: For instance, damage to this region impairs key memory integration behaviors like associative inference in humans (Koscik and Tranel, 2012; Spalding et al., 2018; Warren et al., 2014) and transitive inference in rodents (DeVito et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies in humans.

claim: Damage to medial prefrontal cortex impairs transitive inference in rodents.
source: For instance, damage to this region impairs key memory integration behaviors like associative inference in humans (Koscik and Tranel, 2012; Spalding et al., 2018; Warren et al., 2014) and transitive inference in rodents (DeVito et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies in rodents.

claim: Activation of mPFC increases when encoding episodes containing stimuli that overlap with recently learned information.
source: Furthermore, activation of this region and its connectivity with the hippocampus increases when encoding episodes containing stimuli that overlap with recently learned information (Kuhl et al., 2010; Schlichting and Preston, 2016; Zeithamova et al., 2012), providing convincing evidence of its role in memory integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies of encoding.

claim: Connectivity between mPFC and hippocampus increases when encoding episodes containing stimuli that overlap with recently learned information.
source: Furthermore, activation of this region and its connectivity with the hippocampus increases when encoding episodes containing stimuli that overlap with recently learned information (Kuhl et al., 2010; Schlichting and Preston, 2016; Zeithamova et al., 2012), providing convincing evidence of its role in memory integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies of encoding.

claim: Patterns of activity in mPFC become more correlated for events linked through overlapping elements.
source: Of particular relevance to the current study, patterns of activity in mPFC become more correlated for events linked through overlapping elements (Schlichting et al., 2015; Milivojevic et al., 2015) and also carry information about the common structure across many learned relationships (Morton et al., 2020; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pattern similarity studies.

claim: mPFC patterns carry information about the common structure across many learned relationships.
source: Of particular relevance to the current study, patterns of activity in mPFC become more correlated for events linked through overlapping elements (Schlichting et al., 2015; Milivojevic et al., 2015) and also carry information about the common structure across many learned relationships (Morton et al., 2020; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of representational content in mPFC.

claim: There is much less evidence in humans that neural representations in mPFC are predictive of behavioral measures of memory integration over the course of systems-level consolidation.
source: However, there is much less evidence in humans that the neural representations in mPFC are predictive of behavioral measures of memory integration over the course of systems-level consolidation, despite such strong behavioral evidence of consolidation-dependent behavioral integration (e.g. Chatburn et al., 2014) and the increasing involvement of mPFC in memory retrieval over time (Bonnici et al., 2012; Frankland et al., 2004; Takashima et al., 2006; Takashima et al., 2009; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008; Woodard et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature based on the authors' review and citations.

claim: mPFC involvement in memory retrieval increases over time.
source: However, there is much less evidence in humans that the neural representations in mPFC are predictive of behavioral measures of memory integration over the course of systems-level consolidation, despite such strong behavioral evidence of consolidation-dependent behavioral integration (e.g. Chatburn et al., 2014) and the increasing involvement of mPFC in memory retrieval over time (Bonnici et al., 2012; Frankland et al., 2004; Takashima et al., 2006; Takashima et al., 2009; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008; Woodard et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing time-dependent changes in mPFC involvement.

claim: In rodents, neural ensembles in mPFC become more selective for common features across two different associative memories and less selective to features unique to each.
source: First, in rodents, neural ensembles in mPFC become more selective for common features across two different associative memories and less selective to features unique to each (Morrissey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a rodent electrophysiology study.

claim: There is evidence of delay-dependent changes in the content of memories in human mPFC.
source: Second, there is evidence of delay-dependent changes in the content of memories in human mPFC (Sekeres et al., 2018b; Krenz et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: After a week, neural patterns during the retrieval of overlapping memories grew more correlated in mPFC.
source: Previously, we used a multi-variate pattern similarity approach to demonstrate that after a week, neural patterns during the retrieval of overlapping memories grew more correlated (Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Audrain and McAndrews, 2022 observed an increase in correlation of overlapping memories over time in mPFC.
source: Audrain and McAndrews, 2022 observed a similar increase in correlation of overlapping memories over time in mPFC, although with notable differences in their protocol and consequent findings (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to another study.

claim: Post-learning coordination between hippocampus and cortex can be operationalized by measuring changes in the correlation of their BOLD signals during resting-state fMRI after encoding new memoranda.
source: One way to operationalize such post-learning coordination is by measuring changes in the the correlation of their blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signals during resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) after encoding new memoranda (Tambini et al., 2010; van Kesteren et al., 2010; Tompary et al., 2015; de Voogd et al., 2016; Gruber et al., 2016; Schlichting and Preston, 2016; Murty et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Tambini and D'Esposito, 2020; Audrain and McAndrews, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple resting-state connectivity studies.

claim: Memory-related patterns of coupling are specific to category-selective cortical regions.
source: While hippocampal–cortical coupling is not a direct measure of the reactivation of specific memories, memory-related patterns of coupling are specific to category-selective cortical regions (de Voogd et al., 2016; Murty et al., 2017; Vilberg and Davachi, 2013) and emerge only in post-learning rest periods rather than pre-learning ones, making rest connectivity a likely signature of coordinated reactivation across hippocampus and cortex (Tambini and Davachi, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing category-specific connectivity patterns.

claim: Memory-related patterns of coupling emerge only in post-learning rest periods rather than pre-learning ones.
source: While hippocampal–cortical coupling is not a direct measure of the reactivation of specific memories, memory-related patterns of coupling are specific to category-selective cortical regions (de Voogd et al., 2016; Murty et al., 2017; Vilberg and Davachi, 2013) and emerge only in post-learning rest periods rather than pre-learning ones, making rest connectivity a likely signature of coordinated reactivation across hippocampus and cortex (Tambini and Davachi, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing pre- and post-learning connectivity.

claim: The vast majority of studies investigating post-learning rest connectivity find that the magnitude of experience-dependent change relates to subsequent memory accuracy.
source: The vast majority of studies investigating post-learning rest connectivity find that the magnitude of experience-dependent change relates to subsequent memory accuracy, with the exception of one demonstration that post-learning connectivity relates to explicit associative inference (Schlichting and Preston, 2016).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citations.

claim: Post-learning connectivity relates to explicit associative inference.
source: The vast majority of studies investigating post-learning rest connectivity find that the magnitude of experience-dependent change relates to subsequent memory accuracy, with the exception of one demonstration that post-learning connectivity relates to explicit associative inference (Schlichting and Preston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The earliest demonstration of post-learning connectivity implicated the involvement of category-selective cortex.
source: Beginning with cortex, the earliest demonstration of post-learning connectivity implicate the involvement of category-selective cortex (Tambini et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a foundational study.

claim: Post-learning cortical connectivity with the hippocampus is governed by the category of the encoded memoranda.
source: Numerous findings since then have shown that post-learning cortical connectivity with the hippocampus is governed by the category of the encoded memoranda (Collins and Dickerson, 2019; Keller and Just, 2016; Murty et al., 2017; Schlichting and Preston, 2014; Vilberg and Davachi, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing category-specific effects.

claim: Lateral occipital cortex is causally linked to the formation of object memories.
source: Because our stimuli are common objects, we focused on lateral occipital cortex (LOC), a region causally linked to the formation of object memories (Tambini and D'Esposito, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a causal study.

claim: There is ample evidence that hippocampal interactions with mPFC support integrative encoding.
source: Surprisingly, while there is ample evidence that hippocampal interactions with mPFC support integrative encoding (Zeithamova et al., 2012) and retrieval of remote memories (Takashima et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 2015), there is less evidence that hippocampal coupling with mPFC in post-learning periods leads to strengthening or integration of new memories (Tambini et al., 2010; although cf. Bein et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to encoding studies.

claim: Hippocampal interactions with mPFC support retrieval of remote memories.
source: Surprisingly, while there is ample evidence that hippocampal interactions with mPFC support integrative encoding (Zeithamova et al., 2012) and retrieval of remote memories (Takashima et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 2015), there is less evidence that hippocampal coupling with mPFC in post-learning periods leads to strengthening or integration of new memories (Tambini et al., 2010; although cf. Bein et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to retrieval studies.

claim: There is less evidence that hippocampal coupling with mPFC in post-learning periods leads to strengthening or integration of new memories.
source: Surprisingly, while there is ample evidence that hippocampal interactions with mPFC support integrative encoding (Zeithamova et al., 2012) and retrieval of remote memories (Takashima et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 2015), there is less evidence that hippocampal coupling with mPFC in post-learning periods leads to strengthening or integration of new memories (Tambini et al., 2010; although cf. Bein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citations.

claim: Post-learning hippocampal coupling with mPFC is related to updating and integrating of memories that were either previously strongly learned, older, or consistent with prior knowledge.
source: More commonly, post-learning hippocampal coupling with mPFC is related to updating and integrating of memories that were either previously strongly learned, older, or consistent with prior knowledge (e.g. van Kesteren et al., 2010; Schlichting and Preston, 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Cowan et al., 2020; Audrain and McAndrews, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Post-learning connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortical regions relates to memory for objects and scenes.
source: Here, there are observations that post-learning connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortical regions relate to memory for objects and scenes (Murty et al., 2017; Tambini et al., 2010), whereas connectivity between anterior hippocampus and fusiform face area (FFA) has been shown to relate to memory for faces (Liu et al., 2018) and to explicit associative inferences across stimuli including faces (Schlichting and Preston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining posterior hippocampal connectivity.

claim: Connectivity between anterior hippocampus and fusiform face area relates to memory for faces.
source: Here, there are observations that post-learning connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortical regions relate to memory for objects and scenes (Murty et al., 2017; Tambini et al., 2010), whereas connectivity between anterior hippocampus and fusiform face area (FFA) has been shown to relate to memory for faces (Liu et al., 2018) and to explicit associative inferences across stimuli including faces (Schlichting and Preston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining anterior hippocampal connectivity.

claim: Connectivity between anterior hippocampus and fusiform face area relates to explicit associative inferences across stimuli including faces.
source: Here, there are observations that post-learning connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortical regions relate to memory for objects and scenes (Murty et al., 2017; Tambini et al., 2010), whereas connectivity between anterior hippocampus and fusiform face area (FFA) has been shown to relate to memory for faces (Liu et al., 2018) and to explicit associative inferences across stimuli including faces (Schlichting and Preston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Memory performance for low-reward items is correlated with connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex.
source: Connectivity with anterior or posterior hippocampus also depends on whether memory is rewarded, with memory performance for low-reward items correlated with connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex and memory for high-reward items related to connectivity between anterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex (Murty et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study examining reward effects on connectivity.

claim: Memory for high-reward items is related to connectivity between anterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex.
source: Connectivity with anterior or posterior hippocampus also depends on whether memory is rewarded, with memory performance for low-reward items correlated with connectivity between posterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex and memory for high-reward items related to connectivity between anterior hippocampus and category-selective cortex (Murty et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study examining reward effects on connectivity.

claim: The learning of statistical regularities relies on the hippocampus and benefits from consolidation processes.
source: We made this decision for several reasons: (1) the learning of statistical regularities relies on the hippocampus and benefits from consolidation processes (Durrant et al., 2011; Durrant et al., 2013; Turk-Browne et al., 2009; Schapiro et al., 2012; Schapiro et al., 2014), in line with predictions from TTT
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on statistical learning.

claim: Response times have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration across several domains, including lexical integration of novel word learning.
source: In addition to statistical learning, RTs have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration across several domains, including lexical integration of novel word learning (Bowers et al., 2005; Davis et al., 2009; Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2014), motor learning (Kuriyama et al., 2004; Fischer et al., 2006), and category learning (Hennies et al., 2014), making them an ideal readout of memory integration that minimizes potential on-the-fly retrieval strategies that might inflate rates of integration (Abolghasem et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using RT measures.

claim: Response times have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration in motor learning.
source: In addition to statistical learning, RTs have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration across several domains, including lexical integration of novel word learning (Bowers et al., 2005; Davis et al., 2009; Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2014), motor learning (Kuriyama et al., 2004; Fischer et al., 2006), and category learning (Hennies et al., 2014), making them an ideal readout of memory integration that minimizes potential on-the-fly retrieval strategies that might inflate rates of integration (Abolghasem et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using RT measures.

claim: Response times have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration in category learning.
source: In addition to statistical learning, RTs have been shown to reflect consolidation-dependent memory integration across several domains, including lexical integration of novel word learning (Bowers et al., 2005; Davis et al., 2009; Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2014), motor learning (Kuriyama et al., 2004; Fischer et al., 2006), and category learning (Hennies et al., 2014), making them an ideal readout of memory integration that minimizes potential on-the-fly retrieval strategies that might inflate rates of integration (Abolghasem et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using RT measures.

claim: Participants implicitly encoded sequences of objects with overlapping structure in two experiments.
source: In two experiments, participants implicitly encoded sequences of objects with overlapping structure.
evidence: This describes the experimental design implemented in the study.

claim: Each sequence was constructed such that the first two objects always appeared consecutively (A and B), and the third object alternated between two objects (C1 and C2).
source: Each sequence was constructed such that the first two objects always appeared consecutively (A and B), and the third object alternated between two objects (C1 and C2; Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participants became faster across repetitions during learning.
source: This model revealed an effect of repetition (F(1, 4448) = 1070.17, p < 0.001), reflecting faster responses times as learning progressed
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of response time data during learning.

claim: Participants responded more quickly to predictable objects over unpredictable ones during learning.
source: and an effect of predictability (F(1, 232.4) = 4.48, p = 0.04) such that participants responded more quickly to predictable objects over unpredictable ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of response time data during learning.

claim: There was a steeper drop in response times over learning for predictable objects relative to unpredictable ones.
source: These two effects were qualified by an interaction (F(1, 4448) = 104.73, p < 0.001), reflecting a steeper drop in RTs over learning for predictable objects relative to unpredictable ones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Participants became sensitive to the sequence structure and were faster to respond to predictable objects over unpredictable ones during both recent and remote sessions.
source: Critically, there was no interaction between learning session and predictability or between learning session, predictability, and repetition (both F's < 2.10, both p's > 0.14) suggesting that participants became sensitive to the sequence structure and were faster to respond to predictable objects over unpredictable ones during both sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no interaction effects.

claim: Average accuracy on the size judgment task was high (92.6%; SD = 12.5%) in Experiment 1.
source: Average accuracy on the size judgment task was high (92.6%; SD = 12.5%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: Recognition accuracy across all objects approached perfect performance in Experiment 1.
source: Recognition accuracy across all objects approached perfect performance, as measured by A (Zhang and Mueller, 2005), a non-parametric measure of sensitivity that integrates hits and false alarms and can accommodate perfect performance (remote: mean A = 0.967, SD = 0.043; recent: mean A = 0.967, SD = 0.045).
evidence: This claim is supported by descriptive statistics from the recognition task.

claim: Faster response times were observed for primed objects relative to unprimed objects for remotely learned objects in Experiment 1.
source: Indeed, we found faster RTs for primed objects relative to unprimed objects for the remotely learned objects (F(1, 674.43) = 7.97, p = 0.005) but not the recently learned objects (F(1, 69.12) = 0.37, p = 0.54).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the priming task data.

claim: No priming effect was observed for recently learned objects in Experiment 1.
source: Indeed, we found faster RTs for primed objects relative to unprimed objects for the remotely learned objects (F(1, 674.43) = 7.97, p = 0.005) but not the recently learned objects (F(1, 69.12) = 0.37, p = 0.54).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect for recent learning.

claim: Participants exhibited significant evidence for explicit integration in Experiment 1.
source: We found significant evidence for integration (remote: mean = 0.044, SD = 0.142, t(70) = 2.63, p = 0.01; recent: mean = 0.034, SD = 0.139, t(70) = 2.04, p = 0.046) with no reliable difference across learning sessions (t(70) = 0.46, p = 0.65; Figure 2B, top right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the explicit memory task.

claim: There was no reliable difference in explicit integration across learning sessions in Experiment 1.
source: We found significant evidence for integration (remote: mean = 0.044, SD = 0.142, t(70) = 2.63, p = 0.01; recent: mean = 0.034, SD = 0.139, t(70) = 2.04, p = 0.046) with no reliable difference across learning sessions (t(70) = 0.46, p = 0.65; Figure 2B, top right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between sessions.

claim: Explicit integration was above chance for objects learned remotely in Experiment 2.
source: Integration was above chance for objects learned remotely (mean = 0.628, SD = 0.149, t(23) = 4.21, p < 0.001) and recently (mean = 0.635, SD = 0.155, t(23) = 4.28, p < 0.001) with no difference across the two learning sessions (t(23) = −0.22, p = 0.83; Figure 2B, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the explicit memory task in Experiment 2.

claim: Explicit integration was above chance for objects learned recently in Experiment 2.
source: Integration was above chance for objects learned remotely (mean = 0.628, SD = 0.149, t(23) = 4.21, p < 0.001) and recently (mean = 0.635, SD = 0.155, t(23) = 4.28, p < 0.001) with no difference across the two learning sessions (t(23) = −0.22, p = 0.83; Figure 2B, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the explicit memory task in Experiment 2.

claim: There was no difference in explicit integration across the two learning sessions in Experiment 2.
source: Integration was above chance for objects learned remotely (mean = 0.628, SD = 0.149, t(23) = 4.21, p < 0.001) and recently (mean = 0.635, SD = 0.155, t(23) = 4.28, p < 0.001) with no difference across the two learning sessions (t(23) = −0.22, p = 0.83; Figure 2B, bottom right).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between sessions.

claim: The change in fit between the correlation matrix reflecting neural similarity and the model was significantly negative for remotely learned objects in mPFC.
source: Surprisingly, in mPFC, the change in fit between the correlation matrix reflecting neural similarity and the model was significantly negative for the remotely learned objects (t(23) = −3.06, p = 0.006; Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.024; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pattern similarity data in mPFC.

claim: A negative change score in mPFC reflects a decrease in fit between the multi-voxel patterns and the integration model in the post-learning relative to pre-learning snapshots.
source: A negative change score reflects a decrease in fit between the multi-voxel patterns and the integration model in the post-learning relative to pre-learning snapshots, which means that over a combined period of learning and consolidation, voxels in mPFC differentiated objects that appeared in overlapping sequences, contrary to our prediction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result based on the analysis method.

claim: Over a combined period of learning and consolidation, voxels in mPFC differentiated objects that appeared in overlapping sequences.
source: A negative change score reflects a decrease in fit between the multi-voxel patterns and the integration model in the post-learning relative to pre-learning snapshots, which means that over a combined period of learning and consolidation, voxels in mPFC differentiated objects that appeared in overlapping sequences, contrary to our prediction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern similarity results.

claim: Participants with increased similarity among C pairs from overlapping sequences exhibited a stronger priming effect, but only for pairs learned remotely.
source: We found that participants with increased similarity among C pairs from overlapping sequences exhibited a stronger priming effect, but only for pairs learned remotely (r(22) = 0.57, p = 0.004, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.016).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between neural similarity and behavioral priming.

claim: The relationship between mPFC similarity and priming was not detectable for pairs learned recently.
source: This relationship was not detectable for pairs learned recently (r(22) = −0.30, p = 0.15) and the difference in the two correlations was significant (z = 3.07, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationship for recent learning.

claim: The difference in correlations between mPFC similarity and priming for remote versus recent learning was significant.
source: This relationship was not detectable for pairs learned recently (r(22) = −0.30, p = 0.15) and the difference in the two correlations was significant (z = 3.07, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: C objects belonging to overlapping sequences grew more similar to each other in LOC after recent learning.
source: We found that C objects belonging to overlapping sequences grew more similar to each other after recent learning (t(23) = 3.10, p = 0.005, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.02) but not for the remotely learned objects (t(23) = 0.38, p = 0.71), with no reliable difference across the two (t(23) = 1.98, p = 0.06, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pattern similarity in LOC.

claim: C objects belonging to overlapping sequences did not show increased similarity in LOC for remotely learned objects.
source: We found that C objects belonging to overlapping sequences grew more similar to each other after recent learning (t(23) = 3.10, p = 0.005, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.02) but not for the remotely learned objects (t(23) = 0.38, p = 0.71), with no reliable difference across the two (t(23) = 1.98, p = 0.06, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect for remote learning.

claim: The extent of change in LOC similarity did not relate to behavioral priming across participants.
source: Unlike in mPFC, the extent of this change did not relate to behavioral priming across participants (both r's < 0.3, both p's > 0.14; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing no significant relationships.

claim: There was a reliable increase in rest connectivity between posterior hippocampus and LOC after learning.
source: To first examine broad changes resulting from sequence learning, we collapsed across both recent and remote learning and found a reliable increase in rest connectivity between posterior hippocampus and LOC (t(22) = 2.26, p = 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of resting-state connectivity data.

claim: The increase in rest connectivity between posterior hippocampus and LOC was driven primarily by an increase after remote learning.
source: This increase was driven primarily by an increase in connectivity after remote learning (occurring on Day 1) (t(22) = 2.70, p = 0.01, Bonerroni-corrected p = 0.065) rather than after recent learning (occurring on Day 2) (t(22) = 1.11, p = 0.28), although the extent of these increases were not reliably different from each other (t(22) = 1.23, p = 0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing connectivity changes across sessions.

claim: There was no analogous change in rest connectivity between anterior hippocampus and LOC.
source: This finding was selective to aspects of the posterior hippocampus, as there was no analogous change in rest connectivity between anterior hippocampus and LOC (t(22) = 0.23, p = 0.82).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect for anterior hippocampus.

claim: There was an increase in rest connectivity between LOC and mPFC.
source: Surprisingly, there was an increase in rest connectivity between LOC and mPFC (t(22) = 2.25, p = 0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of resting-state connectivity data.

claim: Participants with a greater change in posterior hippocampal–LOC connectivity exhibited larger priming effects only for sequences from the remote learning session.
source: We found that participants with a greater change in posterior hippocampal–LOC connectivity exhibited larger priming effects only for sequences from the remote learning session (r(21) = 0.56, p = 0.005, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.025) and not the recent learning session (r(21) = 0.09, p = 0.69).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between connectivity and behavioral priming.

claim: Participants with a greater increase in mPFC similarity of overlapping sequences also exhibited a greater increase in rest connectivity immediately post-learning, but only for objects from the remote session.
source: We found that participants with a greater increase in mPFC similarity of overlapping sequences also exhibited a greater increase in rest connectivity immediately post-learning, but only for objects from the remote session (r(21) = 0.42, p = 0.048) and not the recent session (r(21) = −0.18, p = 0.40).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between mPFC similarity and connectivity.

claim: The relationship between mPFC similarity and rest connectivity was reliably stronger for the remote session over the recent session.
source: Furthermore, this relationship was reliably stronger for the remote session over the recent session (z = 2.04, p = 0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: Both the change in mPFC similarity and the change in posterior hippocampal–LOC rest connectivity explained unique variance in recognition priming across participants.
source: This revealed unique contributions of both the change in mPFC similarity (t(1, 20) = 2.37, p = 0.03, semi-partial R2 = 0.39) and the change in posterior hippocampal–LOC rest connectivity (t(1, 20) = 2.13, p = 0.045, semi-partial R2 = 0.43) in explaining recognition priming across participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple regression analysis.

claim: Objects that are linked by overlapping preceding sequences become associated over time.
source: This finding suggests that objects that are linked by overlapping preceding sequences become associated over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the priming results.

claim: The lack of a statistical interaction between priming condition and day suggests caution in interpreting priming as an effect that emerges solely after a delay.
source: While we observed reliable priming only after 24 hr, the lack of a statistical interaction suggests caution in interpreting this as an effect that emerges solely after a delay.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: Across participants, the extent of neural integration in mPFC reflects the extent of behavioral integration across overlapping sequences, but this association only emerges after a period involving consolidation.
source: This suggests that across participants, the extent of neural integration in mPFC reflects the extent of behavioral integration across overlapping sequences, but this association only emerges after a period involving consolidation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between mPFC similarity and behavioral priming.

claim: Objects that appeared separately in time, but shared overlapping antecedents, are integrated in LOC immediately after learning but are differentiated in mPFC after 24 hr.
source: Taken together, we find that although on average, objects that appeared separately in time, but shared overlapping antecedents, are integrated in LOC immediately after learning but are differentiated in mPFC after 24 hr.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the pattern similarity results across regions.

claim: Despite differentiation at the group-level in mPFC, participants with stronger neural integration in mPFC exhibited facilitated behavioral integration as reflected by stronger recognition priming.
source: However, despite this differentiation at the group-level, participants with stronger neural integration in mPFC exhibited facilitated behavioral integration as reflected by stronger recognition priming.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between mPFC similarity and behavioral priming.

claim: The long-term implicit integration across overlapping sequences is selectively related to immediate post-learning rest connectivity between the posterior hippocampus and LOC.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that the long-term implicit integration across overlapping sequences is selectively related to immediate post-learning rest connectivity between the posterior hippocampus and LOC.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the connectivity results and their relationship to behavior.

claim: Both coordinated hippocampal–cortical coupling and cortical learning are markers of consolidation that contribute to the behavioral integration of overlapping memories over time.
source: We interpret these findings as evidence that both coordinated hippocampal–cortical coupling and cortical learning are markers of consolidation that contribute to the behavioral integration of overlapping memories over time.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their overall findings.

claim: Participants viewed sequences of three objects in an incidental encoding task.
source: In two experiments, participants viewed sequences of three objects in an incidental encoding task.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Ninety right-handed, native English speakers participated in Experiment 1.
source: Ninety right-handed, native English speakers participated in this experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Of the 65 participants with intact demographic records in Experiment 1, 42 were female, and the mean age was 23 (range: 18–33).
source: Demographic information was lost for 25 participants; of the 65 with intact records, 42 were female, and the mean age was 23 (range: 18–33).
evidence: This is a description of participant demographics.

claim: Seventy-three participants were included in all analyses for Experiment 1 after exclusions.
source: Twelve participants were excluded: six did not return for the second experimental session; one fell asleep; five ended early due to experimental error. A further 5 participants were excluded due to poor performance on the recognition test (A < 3 SD relative to group average for either recent or remote memory), leaving 73 participants included in all following analyses.
evidence: This describes the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: Twenty-eight right-handed, native English speakers (14 female, mean age: 27.14, range: 20–34) participated in Experiment 2.
source: Twenty-eight right-handed, native English speakers (14 female, mean age: 27.14, range: 20–34) participated in this experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample for Experiment 2.

claim: Twenty-four participants were included in the analyses for Experiment 2 after exclusions.
source: Three participants were excluded due to scanner malfunction, and one withdrew after the first session, leaving 24 participants that were included in the following analyses.
evidence: This describes the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: The stimuli consisted of 100 color images of objects.
source: The stimuli used in this experiment consisted of 100 color images of objects, taken from online databases and used in previous studies (DuBrow and Davachi, 2013; DuBrow and Davachi, 2014).
evidence: This describes the stimulus set used in the experiments.

claim: Medial PFC and LOC were functionally defined from the learning scans using a contrast of predictable versus unpredictable objects.
source: Medial PFC and LOC were functionally defined from the learning scans. Specifically, we sought regions that were sensitive to the transition probabilities of the presented triplets. To identify changes in BOLD signal to objects with different transition probabilities, we entered each learning scan into a separate GLM after preprocessing. Two regressors were generated: predictable (B, C1, and C2), and unpredictable (A, baseline).
evidence: This describes the method for defining ROIs.

claim: Bilateral hippocampus was defined using FSL's automatic subcortical segmentation protocol (FIRST).
source: Bilateral hippocampus was defined using FSL's automatic subcortical segmentation protocol (FIRST), which anatomically defines subcortical regions using each participant's T1 anatomical image.
evidence: This describes the method for defining hippocampal ROIs.

claim: The anterior hippocampus is most often implicated in memory integration during more immediate or online integration of stimuli.
source: However, it is important to note that we based this focus solely on offline connectivity findings. When considering how the long axis of the hippocampus differentially supports memory integration, the anterior hippocampus is most often implicated, albeit during more immediate or online integration of stimuli (Schapiro et al., 2012; Schlichting et al., 2015; Ritchey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies examining anterior hippocampal function.
